PHY 100.title: Conceptual Physics
PHY 100.description: An introduction to physics through a conceptual approach, covering Newtonian mechanics, forces, energy, work, motion, sound, light, optics, waves, fluids, electricity, magnetism, nuclear energy, and radiation, with emphasis on their applications in modern society. (Corequisite: MAT 101)

PHY 101L.title: Principles of Physics I Laboratory
PHY 101L.description: Experimental uncertainty and error analysis, vectors, one dimensional motion, projectile motion, Newton’s Second Law of motion, friction, gravitational potential energy, linear momentum and collisions, rotational motion, gravity, waves, sound, fluid mechanics, heat, and laws of thermodynamics. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 101.

PHY 102.title: Principles of Physics II
PHY 102.description: Electrical potential, forces, and fields, electric current and circuits, magnetic forces and fields, electromagnetic induction, electromagnetic waves, reflection and refraction of light, optical instruments, and a brief overview of special relativity. Prerequisite: PHY 101.

PHY 102L.title: Principles of Physics II Laboratory
PHY 102L.description: Electrical conductors, Van de Graaff generator, electric field and voltage, dielectrics, Wheatstone bridge, Ohm’s Law and Kirchhoff’s Law, basic oscilloscope operations, charging and discharging a capacitor, magnetic field of a cylindrical coil, Lorentz Force, and Faraday’s Law of induction. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 102.

PHY 103.title: Physics for the Life Sciences I
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 103.description: Solids and fluids, the laws of thermodynamics and heat, gas dynamics, vibrations, waves, sound, reflection and refraction of light, mirrors, lenses, and wave optics.

PHY 103L.title: Physics for the Life Sciences I Laboratory
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 103L.description: Error analysis, viscosity, thermal expansion, Boyle’s Law, heat engine, waves on a stretched string, standing waves, geometrical optics, refraction and reflection, mirrors and lenses, interference, and diffraction. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 103.

PHY 104.title: Physic for the Life Sciences II
PHY 104.description: Electric field, electric potential, Gauss’s Law, Capacitance, electric current, Ohm’s Law, magnetic field, Ampere’s Law, electromagnetic induction, relativity, atomic structure, and radioactivity. Prerequisite: PHY 103.

PHY 104L.title: Physics for the Life Sciences II Laboratory
PHY 104L.description: Error analysis, capacitance, dielectric constant, basic oscilloscope operations, Wheatstone bridge, RC and RL circuits, measurements of magnetic induction, Ohm’s Law, transformers, Bragg diffraction, X-ray fluorescence and radioactivity. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 104.

PHY 105.title: Descriptive Astronomy
PHY 105.description: A minimally quantitative, essentially descriptive, introduction to modern Astronomy, Astrophysics and Cosmology. This course covers calculations of distances and time scales; basic physical principles and ideas used in Astronomy/Astrophysics; the solar system; stellar formation, stellar evolution and death; the galaxies; ideas of contemporary Cosmology/the Universe; and the search for life in the Universe.

PHY 107.title: Medical Physics & Dosimetry
PHY 107.description: The course covers physics principles as applied to medical imaging and radiation therapy. Topics include imaging concepts and metrics, ionizing radiation in diagnosis and therapy, radiation exposure and safety, nuclear medicine, radioactivity, the physics of modern radiotherapy techniques, computed tomography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging. This course is in the format of a three-credit lecture session.

PHY 210.title: Physical Optics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 210.description: Wave theory of light, mathematical description of waves, Maxwell’s equations, superposition, interference, reflection and refraction, polarization, coherence, lasers, holography, one-dimensional and two-dimensional Fraunhofer diffraction. Prerequisite: PHY 102

PHY 211.title: Modern Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 211.description: Einstein's special theory of relativity, black body radiation, the Bohr atom, introductory quantum mechanics, atomic and molecular spectra, atomic physics, nuclear physics, and introduction to elementary particles. Prerequisite: PHY 102.

PHY 211L.title: Modern Physics Laboratory
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 211L.description: Determination of Planck’s constant, determination of specific charge (e/m) of an electron, Franck-Hertz experiment, photoelectric effect, line spectra, electron spin resonance, nuclear magnetic resonance, Bragg reflection, X-ray fluorescence, and radioactivity. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 211.

PHY 212.title: Physics of Waves and Vibrations
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 212.description: Wave phenomena, free and forced vibrations, resonance, coupled systems, normal modes of vibrations, wave-like behavior, interference, diffraction, transmission, reflection, and refraction. Prerequisite: PHY 102.

PHY 221.title: Classical Mechanics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 221.description: Vector representation of forces and moments, Newtonian formulation of mechanics, integration of Newtonian equations of motion, Lagrangian formulation of mechanics, Hamilton dynamics, motion of rigid bodies, Newton’s laws applied to translating and rotating rigid bodies, moments of inertia, linear and nonlinear oscillations, chaos, collisions and coupled oscillations. Prerequisite or Corequisite: MAT 113; Corequisite: MAT 220

PHY 231.title: Electronics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 231.description: Combined lecture/lab course that covers DC and AC circuits, capacitors, inductors, diodes, operational amplifiers, logic gates, timers, microcontrollers, and various transducers. Meets four hours per week. Prerequisite: PHY 102.

PHY 241.title: Mathematical Methods for Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 241.description: Vector analysis, linear algebra, Eigenvalue problems, Fourier analysis, ordinary and partial differential equations, linear operators, Sturm-Liouville problems, in addition to probability and statistics. Prerequisite: MAT 113 and MAT 130.

PHY 320L.title: Junior Physics Laboratory
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 320L.description: Experiments cover phenomena in electricity and magnetism, mechanics, electronics, optics, modern physics, and waves. Prerequisite: Junior standing.

PHY 331.title: Thermodynamics and Statistical Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 331.description: Kinetic theory of gases, the First and Second Laws of thermodynamics, Boltzmann distribution, Gibbs distribution, thermal radiation, heat and work, entropy and temperature, phase transitions, thermodynamics functions and their applications. Prerequisite or Corequisite: PHY 212.

PHY 350.title: Electromagnetic Theory I
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 350.description: Electric potential, electric field, magnetic field, Gauss’ Law, Poisson’s equations and Laplace’s equations, electric currents, Faraday’s Law, Lenz’s Law, mutual inductance, and Maxwell’s equations. Prerequisite: MAT 220.

PHY 351.title: Electromagnetic Theory II
PHY 351.description: Applications and principles of electromagnetic theory and optics, Maxwell’s equations, Poisson’s equations and Laplace’s equations, wave propagation, radiation, scattering and relativity. Prerequisite: PHY 350.

PHY 352.title: Quantum Mechanics I
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 352.description: Matrix representation of quantum mechanical operators, one-dimensional quantum mechanics such as the particle on an infinite potential well, reflection and transmission from potential wells, barriers and steps, the finite potential well and the quantum harmonic oscillator, spin, translational and rotational symmetry, Schrödinger equation in one and three dimensions, hydrogen atom, theory of angular momentum, Hermitian operators, commutator brackets, the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, the Pauli exclusion Principle, orbital angular momentum, rotation operation and spin-orbit coupling. Prerequisite: PHY 241 and PHY 211.

PHY 360.title: Advanced Physics Laboratory
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 360.description: Experiments include selected topics in physics. Prerequisite: PHY 220L.

PHY 361.title: Computational Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 361.description: Methods for solving differential equations, stochastic methods and solutions of transcendental equations, Monte Carlo and other simulation methods, modeling and programming techniques, numerical methods, and computational tools to simulate a wide range of physical problems involving nonlinear dynamics and chaos, molecular dynamics, statistical mechanics, and quantum mechanics. Prerequisites or Corequisite: PHY 331, PHY 352.

PHY 389.title: Internship in Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 389.description: Supervised work in a field related to applied physics, in an organization related to physics, or in a research Laboratory, or in an industrial firm, dealing with acoustics consultancy, nanotechnology, geophysics, nanophysics, seismology, petrophysics, metallurgy, radiation protection or other application in physics. Prerequisite: Senior standing.

PHY 420.title: Introduction to Astrophysics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 420.description: Wave theory of light, interference, polarization and superposition, diffraction, interferometers, coherence, and lasers. Prerequisite: PHY 241.

PHY 441.title: Selected Topics
PHY 441.description: Covers advanced topics in physics. Suggested topics include General Relativity, Special Relativity, Einstein field equation, space-time curvature and gravitation. Prerequisite: MAT 220

PHY 452.title: Quantum Mechanics II
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 452.description: Zeeman and Stark Effects, addition of spin and orbital angular momenta, the physics of spin precession, nuclear magnetic resonance, time independent and time dependent perturbation theory, Fermi's Golden Rule, the physics of radiation emitted during atomic transitions, indistinguishable particles in quantum mechanics, the helium atom, scattering theory, partial wave analysis, and the Born approximation. Prerequisite: PHY 352.

PHY 470.title: Solid State Physics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 470.description: Electron in periodic lattice, vibrations and phonons, free-electron theory in metals, crystals, semi-conductors, superconductivity, excitons, plasmons, polarons, lattice dynamics, and magnetic ordering. Prerequisite: PHY 331 and PHY 352.

PHY 499.title: Senior Project
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHY 499.description: Involvement in team projects that involves literature review and research work guided by a faculty member in the Physics Department. The Senior Project will require students to make use of their experience, skills, and scientific background, in a collaborative manner to fulfill the project requirements. Progress report, a final written report and a group oral presentation are required. Prerequisites: Senior Standing and PHY 351, PHY 352.

POL 101.title: Introduction to Political Science
POL 101.description: Introduces students to the central concepts and questions in the field of political science, providing them with a basic understanding of political science as an academic subject, and engaging them with contemporary global issues. The course will examine political ideologies, forms of government, the role of the state and how governments function and are organized. It also exposes students to different worldviews and gives them the opportunity to present their ideas in written and verbal form.

POL 111.title: Classical Political Thought
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 111.description: This course examines the origins and foundations of the Western tradition of political philosophy. The focus is on the social and historical conditions that influenced the development of the Western tradition of political thought. The goal is to explain the development of the Western tradition as historically contingent, but also to show how its concerns can be adapted to different contexts and to new social conditions. During the course of the semester, we will examine some of the main works and ideas of prominent authors such as Plato, Aristotle, Cicero, St. Augustine, Thomas Aquinas and Marsilius of Padua. We will conclude with a reflection on the legacy of these early ideas in our modern world. Preq: POL 101

POL 112.title: Globalization and World Politics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 112.description: An introduction to globalization and its impact on contemporary world politics. The course surveys major 20th-century developments that shaped the global system and examines key actors, structures, and processes, including the global economy, international law, security, and NGOs. Emphasis is placed on how these forces influence current issues such as environmental challenges, human rights, global security, poverty, inequality, and development. The aim of the course is to provide students with a basic understanding of world politics in a globalized world and to allow students to critically engage with contemporary global issues. The other main aim of the course is to empower students to articulate their ideas and arguments about the world around them in a clear, concise, and logical manner. The course will enable students to critically engage with and analyze contemporary global issues.

POL 113.title: Middle East Politics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.

POL 125.title: American Culture, Politics, & Society
POL 125.description: An interdisciplinary introduction to the overall theme(s) of American culture, politics (both domestic and international) and society, covering selected key events commencing from the ‘discovery’ of the Americas in 1492 to the American Revolution and Independence in 1776 to the second presidency of Donald Trump and many historical, political and cultural highlights in-between.

POL 140.title: Comparative Politics
POL 140.description: Comparative politics is one of the major sub-fields of political science, comprising the systematic study of government and politics, by drawing out differences and similarities within and across countries. This course is designed as an introduction to the main concepts, theories and methods used in explaining real-life political phenomena (states, countries, democracy, groups, institutions, events) across time and space. The empirical evidence is drawn from cases in Africa, the Americas, the Middle-East, Asia and Europe.

POL 142.title: Identity Politics
POL 142.description: The rise of identity politics in the 21st century has become an important feature of the globalized world. This course will explore the role identity politics has played in both a historical and contemporary sense in modern international relations. By focusing on the role of identity politics (religions, racial, gender etc.), the course will allow students to explore some of the most fundamental problems confronting international relations.

POL 191.title: Global Climate Change
POL 191.description: This course investigates the theoretical and practical literature on the critical issue of anthropogenic Climate Change / Global Warming. It discusses the causes of Climate Change and the policies and pragmatic means of combating (“mitigation”) and dealing with the consequences (“adaptation”) of Climate Change by individuals, local communities, nation-states, and the world at large. It focuses on understanding the UN 2015 Paris Climate Agreement and the 1992 UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.

POL 200.title: Public Policy
POL 200.description: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of public policy, including subject, concept and theoretics. It covers the processes of policy-making, policy implementation, and evaluation, and the roles of various institutions and actors in shaping public policies. Students will explore real-world policy issues, analyze case studies, and discuss contemporary policy challenges

POL 214.title: Post-Colonialism
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 214.description: ‘Postcolonialism’ generally refers to the study of the histories, politics, economics, literature, and social milieus of nations within Latin and South America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia. These continental regions are also variously referenced as "the Third World" and "the Global South,". The frame of 'postcolonialism' marks scholarship that has placed the history of colonialism and its aftermath at the center of our understandings of these places. The course will explore this by drawing on Marxist politics, theories, and movements from authors including Marx, Trotsky, Gramsci, Marcuse, Althuser, Escobar, Cesaire, Fanon, Nandy etc.

POL 219.title: Colloquium on Machiavelli
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 219.description: This course introduces students to the major works of Machiavelli through the close reading and discussion of his writings in their cultural and historical contexts. Students will encounter Machiavelli’s texts on their own, with guidance from lectures and have the opportunity to react to Machiavelli’s writing before grappling with its reception and interpretation. Students will deepen their understanding of Machiavelli’s thought by considering historical, literary, cultural, artistic, and political-theoretical points of view.

POL 221.title: Intro to Security Studies
POL 221.description: This course is designed as an introduction to Security Studies. Since the late 1980s, there has been a remarkable change in the way security is conceived, studied and practised. Contemporary security issues cut across many barriers—physical, conceptual, and disciplinary. The Globalized world, characterized by the ever-increasing flows of information, capital, goods, services, commerce, people and violence penetrates our local communities and present challenges that may threaten the safety and security of people and institutions. The insecurity that results from these broad-based, cross-cutting, and often invisible pressures demands equally broad-minded inquiry into their causes, their effects, and their potential amelioration. As a result, the academic field of Security Studies has been the subject of intense academic, intellectual and political debate in recent times. The main aim of this course is to introduce students to old and new thinking about Security Studies. It traces the evolution of Security Studies from the study of war and strategy to concerns with individual, societal and global security. The course will focus on the basic concepts central to Security Studies and allow students to gain an introductory overview of the field of Security Studies.

POL 230.title: International Political Economy
POL 230.description: The study of International Political Economy offers a unique opportunity to combine effectively the study of international and domestic politics with the study of economic development, international trade and economic stability. This course will first offer students a coherent view of the development of the International Economic System. This will allow us to then better understand how the International Economic System currently operates. In order to better understand the operation of the modern world economic system, we will focus on a number of key issues and areas of interest, starting with the mechanisms that regulate the international financial system and international trade, and ending with questions related to economic development and the impact of climate change on the future of the World Economy.Preq POL 101

POL 240.title: International Organization
POL 240.description: The course will focus on intergovernmental organizations (IOs) by examining their historical origins, ostensible functions, the international and domestic political forces that impact their operations, and their effectiveness. What role do International Organizations (IOs) play in global politics? Some think their role is trivial. Others argue that they fulfill their important stated purposes. Still others argue that governments use them to pursue their own private goals. The course will address some overarching theoretical and methodological issues so that we have a core set of analytical tools we can apply to our study of specific IOs.

POL 252.title: Iraqi Politics
POL 252.description: Embark on a comprehensive journey through Iraq's intricate history, politics, and societal transformations in this course, Iraqi Politics. The course explores deep into Iraq's evolution from its establishment post-Ottoman Empire collapse in 1921 to its current socio-political landscape. The course discusses challenges the Iraq faced during the 20th and 21st centuries including unity within a diverse society marked by ethno-sectarian divisions. This course chronologically explores historical events, governance structures, and the complexities of forging a national identity, offering invaluable insights into Iraq's enduring struggles and historical roots, surpassing the post-2003 invasion era to paint a holistic portrait of the nation's quest for unity.

POL 253.title: Middle East and Iran
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 253.description: This course, POL 253 Middle East and Iran, provides an in-depth exploration of the modern political history, international relations, and domestic developments in the Middle East, with a special emphasis on Iran. The course examines the historical foundations of state formation, colonial and post-colonial transformations, ideological movements such as nationalism and Islamism, and the region's interaction with global powers. Focusing particularly on Iran, the course analyzes the evolution of its political system, foreign policy strategies, revolutionary changes, and contemporary challenges. Students will engage with key scholarly debates, primary sources, and current events to understand the complexity and diversity of political life in the Middle East and Iran. Course Prerequisites/Co-requisites: POL 101 and POL 140

POL 262.title: Modern Russia
POL 262.description: This course in Modern Russia describes the period from 1917 to the present, from the Russian revolution to the collapse of the Soviet Union, outlining the enormous diversity of people within the Russian imperial framework, the role of religion in Russian society, and shifting forms of governance. The course illustrates key aspects of Modern Russia by identifying political and social changes in this jurisdiction’s shifting boundaries, through assessment of primary and secondary sources.

POL 263.title: Hungary: Socioeconomic History, etc
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 263.description: This course introduces students to the semi-periphery of Europe and more closely, Hungary and its neighbors within and beyond the European Union. The historical component links Hungary to Asia through the initial founding of the state, as well as the Mongol conquest, followed by centuries within the Western world (marked by Roman Catholic as well as Protestant culture), the Ottoman era, Austrian domination, the experience of Austro-Hungary, the disastrous world wars and Nazi occupation, Communism, and a difficult post-Communist transition. Beyond political history, the course deals with issues of culture and the humanities in formerly Habsburg Europe.

POL 265.title: Canadian Foreign and Defense Policy
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 265.description: The study of Canadian foreign and defense policy offers a unique perspective on a host of key issues that have shaped the world in which we live. As a key Western ally, Canada has been part of every major debate, initiative or event, in the areas of peace and security, nuclear weapons and disarmament, diplomacy and peace negotiations, peacekeeping, international development, trade and globalization, environmental politics, sovereignty and international law, decolonization, human rights, and the development of the international structure of collective security and governance, since the end of WWII. As one of the United States’ two closest neighbors, along with Mexico, Canada has also had to learn how to manage its complex and sometimes difficult relationship with the world’s only superpower. In doing so, Canada has developed an approach and a perspective that are increasingly being emulated by a host of other states that are confronted with the same challenges. Finally, studying Canadian Foreign Policy offers invaluable insights as well as a mirror to the American perspective, and makes it possible to explore a different view of key moments that have shaped the development of the modern world, and the way global issues are addressed in an increasingly multipolar world.

POL 266.title: Modern South Africa
POL 266.description: This course introduces students to the spatial, legal, economic, social and political structures that created apartheid in South Africa, and to the factors that led to the collapse of the racist order. We will examine the many forms of Black oppression and, also, the various forms of resistance to apartheid. The course focuses on the history of South Africa, with special emphasis on the period from 1860 to the present day. Students will learn how the unequal society was build and study the transitional process to democracy built on one of the world’s most liberal constitutions. The course will also explore contemporary challenges to the democratic project, including economics, politics, and development.

POL 267.title: Latin American Politics
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 267.description: This course provides a survey of politics in key Latin American countries. The course focuses on the historical, sociological, economic and international context, so that students can better understand the contemporary political debates of Latin America. The course emphasizes the study of the countries of South America, but will also examine the politics of Mexico, of the island nation of Haiti and of Guatemala.

POL 268.title: Politics & History of Central Asia
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 268.description: This course presents the history and politics of Central Asian. The course aims to provide students with understanding of key issues in political and societal developments in these countries. The course will help students to acquire knowledge on the nature of state, politics and society in Central Asia, and develop critical thinking on variations in and drivers of political, economic, social and cultural transformations in this part of the world.

POL 270.title: Political Psychology

POL 285.title: International Human Rights
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 285.description: This course provides a historical, theoretical and practical survey of fundamental issues and topics in the area of International Humanitarian Law. Students will be exposed to essential writings from the International Law tradition, and to modern International Humanitarian Law documents that draw from this tradition. Students will also be invited to examine contemporary and historical cases from the perspective of International Humanitarian Law. Prerequisite: POL 111.

POL 295.title: Professional Development and Leadership Seminar
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 295.description: POL 295 is designed to provide the necessary information for students of International Studies to reflect and hone their skills towards opportunities beyond graduation by way of options in graduate studies, volunteerism, and professional employment in public and private sectors in Iraq and abroad. The course is thus intended to prepare students for academic, professional and leadership trajectories after the completion of their BA degree. Students will learn via reading, listening, reflection writing, querying, debating and role playing on their post-BA and longer-term career options, opportunities and goals. Aside from lectures, assigned readings, interview simulations, practice in public speaking, and resumé building, students will be exposed to guest lectures by individuals and professionals from private and public institutions, international organizations, consulting agencies, and current or former graduate students from primarily European and North American universities. Course Prerequisites/Co-requisites: POL 240 International Organization or POL 312 International Relations

POL 307.title: US Politics & Culture through Film
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 307.description: This course is a study of fundamental political concepts as presented and/or reflected in the medium of motion pictures (film), with an emphasis on strictly political films. Political film is a subgenre of film that emphasizes with political ideas and concepts. Works of political fiction often "directly criticize an existing society or... present an alternative, sometimes fantastic, reality." Prominent works of political film exist in all cultures. For this course, the films will be in the English language, covering the basic concepts of communitarian societies, war and military-political relations, anarchy, dictatorial repression, feminism, environmental issues, etc.

POL 311.title: Modern Political Thought
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 311.description: This course offers a broad survey of essential authors and ideas in the field of Political Philosophy. Through the study of pre-eminent authors and their political theories, students will be given the opportunity to examine how these theories and broader philosophical systems affect our contemporary political debates and our lives. The course also proposes that modern political institutions and practices draw their inspiration and their rationale from the ideas developed by prominent political philosophers in reaction to specific social and historical events and circumstances. Political theory is thus presented as inextricably intertwined with political context and issues. Throughout the semester, students will be invited to explore the works of pre-eminent authors from the Analytical, Continental and American traditions of Political Philosophy, and to assess the contribution made by each of these to what we call Modern Political Thought.

POL 312.title: International Relations: Theory and Practice
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 312.description: This course explores the main topics that the International Relations discipline deals with from foreign policy and security to global governance and the global economy, to show how the theories and concepts help students to make sense of contemporary issues and events. With reference to such diverse events as Brexit, the Russian armed conflict in Ukraine, the financial crisis, the rise of China, and the challenges of identity politics, the course is an introductory one, albeit with a theoretical bent.

POL 340.title: The UN and the EU
POL 340.description: This course explores two major international organizations: the United Nations and the European Union, with an emphasis on the EU. Students will gain foundational knowledge about the UN Charter, its global mission and UN institutional structure, followed by a detailed examination of the 2009 Lisbon Treaties: The Treaty on the European Union and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union. Students identify the EU’s institutional structure, its law making and policymaking processes. The course critically assesses the EU as a unique supranational entity and enumerates its interactions with the UN on issues of global governance, peace, and policy coordination.

POL 342.title: Politics of the Indo-Pacific
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 342.description: This course will examine the recent political events and developments in the Indo-Pacific Region, from the perspectives of International Relations, Comparative Politics, International Political Economy, International Law and Democratic Theory. We will attempt to shed light on current events but also on potential future developments, by making use of historical analysis, economic analysis and strategic analysis. We will also focus on the diplomatic strategies and efforts put in play by the different actors in the region, and beyond the region. As part of our analysis, we will explore the use of the innovative and fruitful concept of triads, in order to better understand the Politics of the Indo-Pacific Region.

POL 350.title: Research Methods
POL 350.description: Research methods can be seen as the bridge allowing to link theoretical considerations and empirical material, sometimes pushing the researcher to downscale his/her ambitions, some others opening up unforeseen avenues for research. Starting from this consideration on the role of methods in social sciences, this course aims to provide students with a thorough understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of the main research methods they are likely to employ when conducting research in social and political science. The course is structured into four parts, focusing respectively on the key debates in the philosophy of social science, on the quantitative research methods, and qualitative research methods, and with a final block about research writing and presentation at the end of the course where students are asked to present the research that they have carried out throughout the semester.

POL 360.title: Quantitative Methods
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 360.description: This course offers a broad introduction to the use of quantitative data analysis and representation in the Social Sciences. Making use of real-world examples from the fields of Political Science, Sociology, Anthropology, Public Policy, and International Relations. Delving into the use of quantitative techniques of representation and analysis, we will examine questions pertaining to the types of data and the types of variables used in research, building and using a sample, the construction and analysis of frequency distributions, the Central Limit Theorem and its use, the relationship between variables and indicators, hypothesis testing, the use of probability measurements, the use of ANOVA and of CROSSTABS, and the development of statistical modeling techniques." Should they choose, students enrolled in the College of International Studies may enroll in "Quantitative Methods" as an alternative to MAT 101, MAT 102, or MAT 111. in fulfillment of the University's general education requirement "Quantitative Reasoning.”

POL 390.title: Seminar: Theoretical & Comparative Issues
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 390.description: This course will explore and discuss a range of research approaches to, and topics in, comparative politics. Students will consider issues related to research design, including comparative methods, case selection, concepts and measures. Then, we’ll focus on specific topics in comparative politics. These topics include economic development and democracy, democratization, authoritarianism, institutional choice, norms/values/culture, comparative political economy, corruption, social movements, and civil conflict.

POL 391.title: Seminar: Security and Democracy
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
POL 391.description: The pressing challenges posed by today’s global political landscape call for changing notions of both security and democracy. How is it possible to provide security for people, states, regions, the globe, and still attend to the basic fundaments of democratic principles? Questions like this evoke even more urgency as it becomes increasingly clear that contemporary threats and risks clearly transgress those borders that have been erected to protect, and to distinguish, friend from foe. This course will address the interlinkages between democracy and security in an everchanging context.

POL 392.title: PPP Internship: Policy, Participation, Practice
POL 392.description: Internships are off-campus experiential learning activities designed to provide students with opportunities to make connections between the theory and practice of academic study and the practical application of that study in a professional work environment. Internships provide entry-level, career-related experience, and workplace competencies that employers value when hiring new employees.

POL 491.description: This course is the final course for the International Studies Program. In this course, finishing students are required to complete a major undergraduate research paper and to demonstrate advanced research skills and in-depth knowledge in the field of International Studies.

PSY 101.title: Introduction to Psychology
PSY 101.description: This course introduces the principles of psychology. It considers sensation, perception, cognition, learning, physiological psychology, personality, development, psychopathology, social psychology, methodology, assessment, and history of psychology with an emphasis on how the science of psychology impacts everyday life.

PSY 210.title: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 210.description: Examines human development, in the cognitive, social and affective domains, from prenatal life through late adulthood. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 220.title: Biopsychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 220.description: Covers the biological underpinnings of behavior, sensation and perception, learning and memory, language, thought, emotions, and neurological and psychological disorders. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 226.title: Personality Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 226.description: The course provides a brief coverage of research methods in the field before delving in depth into the foundational theories and the evidence base for personality assessment. Topics include but are not limited to psychoanalytic, trait, humanistic, and learning theories of personality followed by examining cultural and cross-cultural differences in personality. Also, theories of motivation, emotion, and understanding the self are covered. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 230.title: Cognitive Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 230.description: Deals with the study of attention, memory, learning, language comprehension and production, reasoning, problem solving, and decision making. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 240.title: Social Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 240.description: Explores individual behavior and its determinants in social contexts; topics include social thinking, social influences, social relations, and applications of social psychology in different contexts. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 270.title: Research Methods in Psychology I
PSY 270.description: Covers quantitative research methods, data collection and analysis, and research ethics. Topics include how to read and critically assess a research study, how to develop research questions and write a proposal, the different research designs commonly used in psychological research, and how to design a survey and develop a robust sampling procedure. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 301.title: Research Methods in Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.

PSY 310.title: Analysis of Psychological Data
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 310.description: Provide an understanding of the selection and use of appropriate statistical tests of quantitative data along with the interpretation. Topics include data and distributions, probability and sampling, descriptive statistics, hypotheses testing, and statistical tests. Course includes lab sessions, for students’ practice. Cross-listed with Statistics for Social Sciences course. Cross-listed with Statistics for Social Sciences. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 320.title: Psychology of Learning
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 320.description: Covers learning theories and principles and how they can be used to modify behavior. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 324.title: Sensation and Perception
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 324.description: The course will be divided into examining the biological bases of sensation and the accompanying perception processes related to vision, hearing, smell, touch, and taste. The course will also be supplemented by the research methods used to study perception and through discussing clinical cases. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 330.title: Organizational Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 330.description: Provides a broad coverage of organization psychology, the scientific study of how individuals behave at work and all the factors that influence their behavior. Topics include focus and research methods in organizational psychology; job analysis; employee’s selection and hiring, performance evaluation, training and development; worker motivation; job satisfaction; organizational communication and group processes; leadership and supervision; and organizational culture. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 332.title: Health Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 332.description: After introducing the different models of health and health outcomes, the course will examine how different factors (e.g., at the individual or policy level) influence health outcomes. The course will also explore topics such as health promotion, disease prevention, psychological adaptation to chronic and infectious illnesses, by using specific illnesses for illustration. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 334.title: Positive Psychology
PSY 334.description: By addressing the history of the positive psychology field, the course will critically examine current research on the correlates and determinants of personal strengths, resilience, humor, emotional intelligence, happiness, forgiveness, compassion, and life satisfaction, among other topics.

PSY 340.title: Cultural Psychology
PSY 340.description: Covers the foundations, theories, findings, and research methods in cultural psychology, the study of how and why culture influences individual’s thinking, emotions, and behavior. Topics include culture and the self, culture and social behavior, culture and cognition, culture and emotion, culture and mental health, acculturation, multiculturalism, stereotypes and biases. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 345.title: Educational Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 345.description: Educational Psychology is the study of how humans learn and retain knowledge in educational settings, such as the classroom. The course focuses on research-based concepts and principles of human learning, development, and motivation by exploring applicable psychological theories in the science of psychology. Students are introduced to theories and research in educational and learning practices. Current views of educational issues will be examined with an emphasis on the complex interaction between social, cognitive, behavioral, and societal factors involved in formal educational settings. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 350.title: Abnormal Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 350.description: The course explores major theories, risk factors, and diagnoses of mental disorders such as anxiety, mood, substance-use disorders, personality disorders, psychosis, and post-traumatic stress disorder, providing a comprehensive understanding of abnormal psychology. Emphasis is placed on etiologies, symptoms, and societal misconceptions, fostering a holistic perspective on mental health challenges. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 360.title: Cognitive Science
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 360.description: Drawing upon different fields such as neuroscience, cognitive psychology, linguistics, philosophy, artificial intelligence, and others, the aim of the course is to understand how each discipline has contributed to the emergence and development of the field of how the mind works. Topics include but are not limited to information processing, language acquisition, and consciousness. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 370.title: Research Methods in Psychology II
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 370.description: Covers qualitative research methods, data collection and analysis, and research ethics. Topics include observational methods, interviewing, diary and narrative methods, focus groups, interpretative phenomenological analysis, grounded theory, discourse analysis, content analysis, and writing up research. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 390.title: Internship I in Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 390.description: Provides the student with an applied structured learning experience in a professional/ work setting under the supervision of a faculty member. Prerequisite: PSY 101, and junior standing.

PSY 420.title: Clinical psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 420.description: This course provides an introduction to the field of Clinical Psychology, exploring the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of psychological disorders. Students will examine major theoretical approaches, including cognitive, behavioral, psychodynamic, and humanistic therapeutic models, while gaining an understanding of evidence-based practices. Topics will also touch on the history of clinical psychology, ethical and cultural considerations, child and adolescent therapy, and the role of research in guiding practice. Course Prerequisites: PSY 101 Course Corequisites: None

PSY 431.title: Psychology of Gender
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 431.description: The course will synthesize findings across different disciplines to examine differences in gender, sex, and sexuality, illustrate how processes of school and family socialization, employment, and interpersonal relationships impact gender differences. A focus on the role of gender in the Arab world will also be addressed. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 440.title: Special Topics in Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 440.description: This course offers an in-depth study of selected topics in human behavior and psychology. Topics vary each semester according to the specialization of faculty members and emerging areas of study. Prerequisite: Consent of instructor.

PSY 450.title: Introduction to Trauma Studies
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 450.description: An in-depth multi-disciplinary course that tackles the history of the trauma diagnosis, the biological and psychological development to trauma-related disorders, the effects of exposure to traumatic events on interpersonal relationships, family dynamics, and subsequent development of other disorders such as substance use, dissociative disorder, and borderline personality disorder. The course will also cover the recent literature on complex trauma, among children and adults, and how communities and mental health services can create an environment conducive to recovery. Prerequisite: PSY 350.

PSY 453.title: Counseling Psychology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 453.description: The introductory course to counseling psychology will start with an overview of the field, differences between counseling and clinical psychology, followed by the theories and applications of counseling psychology across different settings (e.g., community and educational counseling services). Prerequisite: PSY 351, OR PSY 352.

PSY 455.title: Behavioral Neuroscience
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 455.description: The aim of the course is to explore the structures and functions of the nervous system and their connection to behavior. Topics include but are not limited to neuroanatomy, research using psychophysiological methods, wakefulness and sleep, and drug addiction. Prerequisite: PSY 101.

PSY 460.title: Cognitive Neuroscience
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 460.description: The course is designed to explore the neural processes associated with mental process or cognition such as language, memory, attention, and emotions by first introducing the research methods used within the field of cognitive neuroscience and then relating them to the knowledge produced by the field. Prerequisite: PSY 360.

PSY 465.title: Psychology and Technology
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PSY 465.description: This course will examine the evolving relationship between psychology and technology, with attention to both 1) how digital innovations influence cognitive, affective, and behavioral outcomes, and also 2) how concepts from the field of psychology inform the design and use of technology. Students will also explore key topics such as social identity and behavior in online and virtual spaces, persuasion and manipulation through technology, and the ethical use of psychological data in tech applications. The course touches on emerging topics, such as artificial intelligence, virtual reality, and digital mental health tools. Through interactive discussions, empirical research, and hands-on activities, students will critically analyze current technological trends through a psychological lens. UG Course Prerequisites: PSY 101 UG Course Co-requisites: None

RAD 101.title: Introduction to Radiologic Sciences
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 101.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive overview of the field of radiologic sciences and technology. This course covers the history and evolution of medical imaging, the various imaging modalities including X-ray radiography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and nuclear medicine imaging, and the principles of radiation physics and protection. The students will also learn about patient care and communication, medical ethics, and legal considerations in the field. This course makes use of a didactic combination of lectures, discussions, demonstrations, and hands-on experiments to introduce the student to topics in Radiologic Sciences.

RAD 201.title: Medical imaging systems I
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 201.description: The course on medical imaging Systems I focuses on providing a comprehensive understanding of the principles, practices, and technologies involved in ionizing radiation imaging with focus on X-ray radiography and computed tomography (CT) imaging systems. The course covers the basics of conventional and digital radiography (DR), CT, fluoroscopy, mammography, and Cathlab imaging systems and how they are used to diagnose and treat various medical conditions. The course will delve into the physics and instrumentation involved in both radiography/fluoroscopy and computed tomography imaging and how these techniques are used in medical imaging. The course will provide hands-on experience and practical training in the use of ultrasound and radiography imaging equipment and will cover the various applications of these imaging systems in clinical practice. Prerequisite: RAD 101.

RAD 210.title: Contrast Agents and Radiopharmaceuticals
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 210.description: This course focuses on the study of contrast agents and radiopharmaceuticals used in medical imaging and nuclear medicine with emphasis on pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. The course covers the basic principles and properties of contrast agents and radiopharmaceuticals, including their mechanism of action and applications in medical imaging including intravenous, intra-arterial, intra-ductal, and intrathecal routes. Students will learn about the different types of contrast agents, including those used in computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), fluoroscopic and ultrasound imaging and nuclear medicine imaging. Prerequisite: RAD 101.

RAD 301.title: Medical Imaging Systems II
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 301.description: The course of Medical Imaging Systems with a focus on Non-Ionizing Imaging Modalities will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles, techniques, and applications of nonionizing medical imaging. The course will emphasize the study of Ultrasound and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) modalities. Students will learn about the physical and technical aspects of ultrasound topics include: propagation of ultrasonic waves in biological tissues, acoustic impedance, modulation transfer function and tissue harmonics, in addition to the principles of ultrasonic measuring and imaging instrumentation, design and use of contemporary tools for performance evaluation of diagnostic instrumentation, and biological effects of ultrasound the principles of sound waves and their interactions with biological tissues. They will also study the different types of ultrasound imaging, including real-time in A-Mode, B-Mode, C-Mode, M-Mode and Doppler imaging, and their clinical applications. The course will also introduce the students to the principles of MRI operation, including the principles of magnetic resonance, spectroscopic localization, spin magnetization and the techniques used in MRI imaging, MRI sequences, such as proton density (PD) -weighted (T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and contrastenhanced MRI, and their applications in different clinical imaging scenarios.

RAD 305.title: Imaging Procedures I
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 305.description: This course provides the student with the knowledge and skills to practice medical imaging in a simulated clinical environment and will focus on the optimization patient positioning and proper operation of imaging equipment of plane X-ray radiography, computerized radiography (CR), fluoroscopy, and computed tomography (CT) and mammography imaging. Moreover, students will learn to achieve the highest image quality with the best contrast-to-noise ratio and quickest scan time for different imaging procedures. The course also addresses ultrasonography and radionuclide imaging. This course includes laboratory exercises with hands-on practical applications for topics discussed in the course. The course will also cover the importance of minimizing radiation exposure to the patient while still obtaining the best possible image quality. The students will be equipped with the knowledge and skills needed to implement best practices in imaging procedures, thereby improving patient outcomes, and optimizing the use of resources in healthcare. Prerequisite: RAD 210.

RAD 305L.title: Imaging Procedures I Lab
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 305L.description: The laboratory part of RAD 305 Imaging Procedures I. Prerequisite or corequisite: RAD 305.

RAD 310.title: Radiographic Anatomy and Pathology I
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 310.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the anatomy and pathology of the human body as it relates to ionizing radiation imaging modalities. The course will focus on conventional radiography, fluoroscopy, mammography, and computed tomography (CT) imaging, with an emphasis on the anatomy and pathological conditions of various body systems. Students will learn the anatomy of various organ systems and the radiological appearance of normal and abnormal conditions, including the recognition and interpretation of common pathological conditions. The course will also cover the principles of imaging modalities and the impact of patient positioning and imaging techniques on image quality. The course will use a combination of lectures, imaging case studies, and hands-on experience to provide students with a solid foundation in the anatomy and pathology of the human body as it relates to ionizing radiation imaging modalities. Prerequisite: BIO 218.

RAD 315.title: Legal and Ethical Aspects in Radiologic Sciences
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 315.description: This course offers the student a study of legal and ethical issues in radiologic sciences. Topics include patient safety, informed consent, confidentiality, professional conduct, ethical theories, end of life care, living wills, confidentiality, risk management and radiology reporting quality review, Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and implementation of the electronic health record. Prerequisite: RAD 101

RAD 355.title: Imaging Procedures II
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 355.description: This course provides students with hands-on training in non-ionizing radiation imaging procedures, specifically in the areas of ultrasonography and echocardiography. The course will focus on patient positioning and imaging protocols, including the selection of appropriate probes, optimization of signalto-noise ratio (SNR) and modulation transfer function (MTF), as well as the use of tissue harmonics, timeof-flight (TOF), and optimal frequency selection for improved resolution. Students will also learn about different ultrasound and echocardiography imaging procedures and applications, including special needs patients and pediatrics. Prerequisite: RAD 301, RAD 305 and RAD310.

RAD 355L.title: Imaging Procedures II Lab
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 355L.description: The laboratory part of RAD 355 Imaging Procedures II. Prerequisite or corequisite: RAD 355.

RAD 362.title: Clinical Best Practice
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 362.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the best practices and protocols used in clinical radiology settings. The course will cover various aspects of patient care and management, including patient preparation, imaging protocols, and equipment usage. Students will learn about the importance of following established guidelines and standards to ensure patient safety and produce highquality images. The course will also cover the use of radiation protection measures and techniques to minimize patient exposure to ionizing radiation. Additionally, students will learn about effective communication with patients and peers in the workplace and the skills needed to provide safe and best standard of care in radiology services. Prerequisite: RAD 315.

RAD 365.title: Introduction to Radiation Therapy
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 365.description: This course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive overview of the principles and practices of radiation therapy (RT). The course will cover the history and evolution of radiation therapy, the role of radiation therapist, the various modalities of radiation therapy including external beam radiation therapy, brachytherapy, and systemic radiation therapy, and the clinical applications of radiation therapy in the treatment of cancer. Students will learn about the anatomy and physiology of the human body and the effects of radiation on different tissues and organs. The course will also cover the principles of radiation therapy dosimetry, conformal mapping, external beam radiation therapy, brachytherapy, proton therapy, stereotactic radiosurgery. Students will also learn about the principles of Radiation Therapy treatment planning, including image simulation, RT treatment planning, and treatment delivery. The course will provide hands-on experience with various treatment planning systems and treatment delivery equipment (Gamma Knife, Linear accelerator (LINAC), and Proton beam therapy (PBT)). The focus of the course will be on the safe and effective administration of Radiation Therapy and the importance of quality assurance in the radiation therapy and planning process. Prerequisite: PHY 107.

RAD 370.title: Computer Applications in Medical Imaging
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 370.description: This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of computer-based image processing and analysis techniques in medical imaging. The students will learn about the different methods used for image processing and analysis, including thresholding, edge detection, morphological operations, pattern recognition, 2D/3D rendering, and region-based segmentation. They will also learn how to apply these techniques to medical imaging data of Radiography, mammography, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), positron emission tomography/single-photon emission computed tomography (PET/SPECT) to improve the accuracy and efficiency of diagnosis and treatment. In addition to the theoretical concepts, students will also get hands-on experience with various software tools and programming languages used in medical imaging. They will learn how to use 3D Slicer, MATLAB, ImageJ, and other similar tools for medical image processing and analysis. Prerequisite:

RAD 390.title: Practicum I: Internship in Clinical Imaging
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 390.description: Practicum I: Internship in Clinical Imaging This practical training course requires that the student spends around 135 hours of supervised experience in a medical imaging center. The course correlates the acquired academic concepts into the clinical environment, dealing directly with patients. Under the supervision of a radiologist, the student is offered the opportunity to observe and perform medical imaging of different human body parts. Clinical competency assessment and evaluations are utilized to document the clinical performance of the student. Prerequisite: RAD 355 and RAD 315.

RAD 405.title: Imaging Procedures III
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 405.description: This course focuses on the application of non-ionizing radiation imaging modalities, specifically Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), in a clinical setting. The course will not cover the physics of MRI, but instead will concentrate on the practical aspects of MRI imaging procedures and patient positioning techniques. The students will learn how to select the best body RF coils, tune physical imaging parameters, maximize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), manage, and minimize various imaging artefacts, handle special needs and pediatric patients, and set up the anesthesia in the MRI clinical environment. The course will provide hands-on experience to the students in optimizing MRI imaging sequences and protocols to achieve highquality imaging results. Prerequisite: RAD 305.

RAD 405L.title: Imaging Procedures III Lab
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 405L.description: The laboratory part of RAD 405 Imaging Procedures III. Prerequisite or corequisite: RAD 405.

RAD 410.title: Special Topics in Radiological Sciences
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 410.description: This course focuses on the latest developments in medical imaging modalities, including positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), positron emission tomography/magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI), single-photon emission computed tomography/positron-emission tomography (SPECT/PET), spectral imaging, medical thermography imaging, and optical imaging. Students will gain a comprehensive understanding of these cutting-edge imaging techniques and their applications in medical diagnosis and treatment. The course will cover the principles and theories behind each modality, as well as their clinical applications, strengths, and limitations. Through a combination of lectures, hands-on laboratory experience, and case studies, students will develop the skills and knowledge necessary to effectively use these advanced imaging modalities in clinical settings. Prerequisite: RAD 365 and RAD 370.

RAD 420.title: Radiology Quality Assurance Laboratory
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 420.description: The course provides students with hands-on experience in performing calibration and verification procedures for X-ray radiography detectors and imaging modalities. This lab course is designed to give students a thorough understanding of the fundamental concepts and practical skills involved in ensuring quality in radiology imaging. The focus is on X-ray detector calibration and verification, which involves adjusting the detector to produce optimal image quality, and imaging modalities calibration and verification, which involves testing and adjusting the imaging equipment using radiology phantoms devices to ensure that it is operating correctly and producing accurate images. The course will delivers in-depth knowledge of the various parameters that impact image quality, such as spatial resolution, contrast resolution, and signal-to-noise ratio, and how to optimize these parameters through calibration and verification procedures. The course will also cover quality control procedures for other imaging modalities, such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the knowledge and skills needed to perform quality assurance (QA) procedures in a clinical setting. Prerequisite: RAD 355 and RAD 370.

RAD 450.title: Practicum II: Internship in Clinical Imaging

RAD 460.title: Nuclear Medicine Imaging
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.
RAD 460.description: This course is designed to introduce students to the field of nuclear medicine, a subspecialty of radiology that uses small amounts of radioactive material to diagnose and treat various diseases and conditions. The course covers the physical principles, concepts, and applications of nuclear medicine imaging, including the use of radiopharmaceuticals, nuclear imaging instrumentation, and various imaging techniques such as single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) and positron emission tomography (PET). Prerequisite: PHY 107.

RAD 480.title: Radiology Information Systems
notices: Taken from the College of Healthcare Technology curriculum (Radiologic Sciences, Appendices III and IV). This course is not in the SIS course catalog yet, so confirm it with the college.

The students will engage in a range of learning activities that encourage critical thinking, analysis, and application of course content. The course will cover topics such as computer systems in radiology, the use of Health Level Seven International ( HL7) interfaces, Health Insurance Probability and Accountability Act (HIPPA), Digital Imaging and Communication in Medicine (DICOM) protocols, and radiology database structures, management and storage, electronic health records, Picture Archiving and Communication S(PACS), and radiology information systems (RIS). The course will also include hands-on training and case studies to provide students with practical experience in utilizing radiology information systems. Prerequisite: MIS 101 and RAD 370.
